title: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
desc: Separates product counts, adoption and revenue while scrutinizing consolidation, model-provider entry and agentic marketing labels.

kps.k: The cluster frames legal AI as an expanding, increasingly complex market that requires disciplined selection and implementation—not simply more product announcements.
kps.d: The substantive commentary comes chiefly from Legal Technology Hub’s Nikki Shaver, Stephanie Wilkins and Sam Moore, often in promotional podcast openings rather than interviews with the named guests. Their shared proposition links proliferating tools and faster feature development to greater demand for market intelligence, workflow-specific procurement and adoption support. Directory tracking, advisory experience and conference observations underpin this account; they do not establish industry-wide productivity or client outcomes.

qs.q: It was already a tough market to navigate when all you had to worry about were the thousands of legal applications; now you also need to track what’s happening in the broader tech ecosystem.
qs.a: Why AI Will Create More Legal Work, Not Less: Filevine's Rizner and Anderson on Research, Access, and Human Judgment · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: But really, we’re, you know, I think we’re at a phase right now where we’ve got to start looking at how attorneys are using this in their day-to-day practice.
qs.a: Alex Su and Andy Chagui on Flexible Legal Talent, AI Pressure, and the Future of Law Firm Leverage · AI-native providers · 2026

kps.k: Successive market maps document expanding coverage, but cannot establish equivalent growth in launches, adoption or revenue.
kps.d: LTH’s generative-AI map progressed from 400 listings in early 2025 to 638 product placements in June, 855 placements from 682 vendors at December 2025, and approximately 1,000 placements in March 2026. These updates describe the same tracking effort, not independent corroboration. Wilkins explains that previously unknown companies and features account for some additions and that coverage depends on what LTH knows. Product placements, vendors and the broader legal-tech directory’s totals are distinct counting units.

qs.q: And so we published that in the beginning of March and we got such an overwhelming response, either from companies we didn’t know about or companies who had Gen.AI features that we didn’t know about, that we decided to rush and do another update to the map just two weeks later to coincide with Legal Week.

qs.q: At that point in time, we saw 638 Genai product placements by 505 vendors in 19 different categories, which was actually 100 more products than we saw just three months before.
qs.a: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey: 'the models are the product', ROI, and turning firm expertise into saleable models · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: The reported product mix is shifting toward operational needs and specialised workflows, without establishing that broad assistants are declining overall.
kps.d: Shaver describes concentrated startup activity moving from broad legal assistants toward intake, compliance and governance in December 2025; Wilkins subsequently identifies operations and compliance as leading growth areas while noting continued assistant growth. Shaver tentatively attributes the shift to crowding in the assistant category. Litigation fact management, fund formation and transaction management illustrate more targeted applications. Claims of better precision, efficiency and collaboration remain qualitative or introductory rather than comparative performance findings.

qs.q: In December, interestingly, that had cooled a little bit and the hot concentration of startup activity had shifted over into operational tools.
qs.a: From Legal Aid to LIT Lab: Quinten Steenhuis and the Builder’s Approach to AI · Academia · 2026

qs.q: And while there still is some growth there, this time around we’re seeing our biggest areas of growth in more bread and butter or less trendy areas, if you will, like law firm operations and compliance.
qs.a: From Document Review to Fact Intelligence, Gregory Mostyn on How Wexler.ai Is Reshaping Litigation · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Continued expansion competes with consolidation concerns, while frontier-model providers complicate the specialist-platform proposition.
kps.d: Shaver rejects the view that generative AI will disappear as a fringe technology and predicts continued investment. Wilkins accepts that consolidation might eventually shrink the map but forecasts 1,500 placements for the second quarter of 2027. These are expectations, not established market outcomes. Separately, reported offerings from Anthropic, Microsoft and Perplexity raise an unresolved question: should buyers replace specialist applications such as Harvey and Legora or combine them with broader platforms? Integrations and specialist fundraising demonstrate commercial activity, not which approach performs better or will control lawyers’ primary workspace.

qs.q: It’s really when being built into so many products that if your practice uses any kind of technology, inevitably you will also  be using generative AI.
qs.a: RAG is Not Dead: Josef's Sam Flynn on Legal Tech That Works · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: given all the consolidation in the market, that may one day be true, but by all accounts, by everything we’re seeing, that we’re not at that point yet.
qs.a: From Document Review to Fact Intelligence, Gregory Mostyn on How Wexler.ai Is Reshaping Litigation · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Agentic marketing requires capability-specific scrutiny rather than acceptance of product labels.
kps.d: LTH reports more than 100 products with announced or partial agentic functionality. Separately, Shaver reports a panel’s conclusion that very few products qualified under Dan Hoadley’s stricter definition: tool use, reasoning, planning, adaptive execution and recognition of completion. Different definitions and reporting moments prevent treating these statements as directly contradictory counts. Shaver’s practical recommendation is to ask whether users can inspect and redirect an agent’s plan before execution; the excerpts do not establish that listed products offer those controls.

qs.q: And LTH has just had what we call our agents week, which just meant lots of different kinds of content dedicate  dedicated to this trend, including an excellent article by Stephanie Wilkins diving into the definition of agents, a timeline of major agentic announcements in legal tech, and our map, which shows already over 100 products in legal that now include some form of agentic AI.
qs.a: Max Junestrand and Ilona Loginova: How Cleary Gottlieb & Legora Are Redefining Legal Work · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: True agents are able to come up with a plan about how to accomplish the overall goal, then pursue that plan and make adjustments to the plan during execution, and they will know when the overall goal is accomplished.
qs.a: Laura Clayton McDonnell on Legal Technology, AI, and Corporate Transformation at Thomson Reuters · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Deployment, actual use and effective workflow adoption remain separate measures.
kps.d: Shaver challenges the assumption that an approachable chat interface makes adoption automatic. She cites unidentified studies reporting firm-wide rollout at approximately 70% of AmLaw 100 firms and adoption around 25%, but the excerpt supplies neither definitions nor methodology. Lambert separately reports a Law360 survey in which 62% of respondents used ChatGPT for legal work; Gebauer questions what respondents counted as legal work. These figures cannot be combined into a common adoption rate. Advisory accounts point instead to training, cultural obstacles, management–lawyer readiness gaps and policy enforcement as practical implementation issues.

qs.q: So recent studies have indicated that although approximately 70 % of the AmLaw 100  firms have rolled out some form of generative AI firm-wide, adoption rates of that technology hover around 25%.
qs.a: Fighting for Your Light: Anusia Gillespie on AI, Legal Innovation, and the Soul Toll of Law · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: One of the things that I just saw that crossed my desk this morning was this survey that Law360 did that showed where, like, 62% of lawyers surveyed and, and I think the metrics were 400 attorneys from large, us, large law firms, but 62% of them say that they use ChatGPT for their, you know, basically their legal work, you know.
qs.a: Front-Stabbing the Future: AI, Law, and the Global Unraveling of Rules with Sean West · Market & press · 2025

kps.k: Procurement increasingly requires assessing actual value, usage costs and control—not just subscription price or activity.
kps.d: Moore describes renewal assessments that examine where tools generate business value and why, rather than presuming that purchase warrants renewal. His client observations link indiscriminate model selection and crowded context windows to delays, token limits and expensive overages. Wilkins reports consumption-based pricing for Legora’s Agent Pro and predicts wider adoption of that pricing model. Shaver’s account of Harvey token growth attributes it to both adoption and product complexity, so token consumption alone cannot measure useful uptake. These accounts support cost-awareness and workflow assessment, but supply no quantified savings or return-on-investment results.

qs.q: And they’ll engage us to run a similar kind of sprint format with a different discovery focus, and we’ll help them surface where that existing tool is and isn’t generating value for the business, help the firm understand why that might be,  and then provide them with the kind of objective understanding needed to really inform that go, no-go decision on renewal.
qs.a: Greg Mazares Sr. on AI, E-Discovery, and the Future of Human-Led Legal Services · AI-native providers · 2026

qs.q: I’ve seen law firm clients whose users just pick the most sophisticated model for everything, toggle on every optional feature available, and then are confused as to why responses are taking a long time and why they’re hitting token limits very, very quickly.

kps.k: Market intermediaries present tailored research and implementation support as a response to buyer and vendor information gaps.
kps.d: LTH promotes maps, feature comparisons, security and hosting information, pilot guides, demonstrations, portfolio tools and advisory services. Shaver argues that mid-sized firms need differentiated guidance because boutiques, volume-litigation practices and regional full-service firms have different requirements. Vendor-facing resources address long sales cycles, security questionnaires and market segmentation. These offerings make the cluster’s practical prescription concrete: define the business problem, compare relevant capabilities and controls, and test organisational fit. Claims that LTH’s services save effort, remain independent or improve outcomes come from the provider or endorsing hosts, not independent evaluations.

qs.q: For each premium category, we have a landscape overview, an evaluation framework, a use case, a pilot guide, a requirements template, and then any other information we think is important.
qs.a: Lawyer 3.0 and the Milkshake Test: Ray Brescia on Legal AI, Client Value, and the Next Wave of Lawyering · Academia · 2026

qs.q: We also touch on security, data privacy, and data hosting information for each of the products.
qs.a: Philip Young of Garfield.AI: The World’s First AI Law Firm Gets the Green Light · AI-native providers · 2025

kps.k: Business-model transformation remains a prospective extension of the market-maturity argument, not a demonstrated consequence.
kps.d: Wilkins reports AI-centred law firms and describes Pierson Ferdinand’s partner-only model as an example of organising service delivery around AI rather than adding an AI committee. Shaver anticipates workflow-level pricing and a premium for trusted judgment, while retaining hourly calculations as an input to alternative fees. These claims broaden the discussion beyond efficiency, but reported firm structures and predictions do not establish superior client outcomes, widespread associate displacement or the disappearance of hourly billing. Many other episode openings merely announce discussion topics; they provide no additional evidence for those conclusions.

qs.q: And the commonality of all of them is that they place AI at the center of their legal service delivery.
qs.a: Women + AI Summit, Real Talk: Leadership, Learning, and Not Letting “The Trap” Write Your Story · Academia · 2026

qs.q: both at law firms where there’s the potential for pricing changes, a lot of momentum towards looking at the value of legal work, not by the billable hour, although the billable hour will still be essential for calculating alternative fee arrangements, but more about how do you really look at individual workflows and what makes sense from a pricing perspective for those workflows.
qs.a: Pablo Arredondo and Joel Hron on Reasoning Models, Deep Research, and the Future of Legal AI · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

vlens.an: The supplied excerpts do not establish how an access-to-justice and civil-society professional voice relates to the proposition. Despite one episode’s access-to-justice framing and named guest, its available material consists chiefly of Nikki Shaver’s vendor-map commentary and the hosts’ promise to move beyond Big Law efficiency and corporate legal-department savings; it contains no substantive contribution from Sateesh Nori about legal aid, housing court or LawDroid. The other excerpt is an event promotion aimed at mid-sized law firms rather than civil-society or access-to-justice users. What evidence is present directionally supports parts of the proposition: one excerpt distinguishes a large mapped landscape and observes a shift toward operational tools, while the other stresses learning what solutions exist and how to deploy them. But neither develops the proposition’s central requirement of disciplined, workflow-specific selection from an access-to-justice perspective. Internal variation is therefore limited to market tracking in the first source and practical implementation education in the second, not substantive disagreement within this professional voice.

qs.q: It has 855 generative AI product placements by 682 vendors across 19 categories, which is obviously a massive landscape now.
qs.a: Sateesh Nori Joins LawDroid: AI Tools for Access to Justice, Housing Court, and Legal Aid · Access to justice · 2026

qs.q: Now for those who don’t know, our mid-law events are pitched at law firms from 20 to 250 lawyers, and they have wonderful content for the entire day for managing partners, office managers, lawyers, about how generative AI can be used to grow your business, how to deploy it, what kinds of solutions are available in the market.
qs.a: The Cytator Strikes Back: Kara Peterson & Rich DiBona On Descrybe’s Fresh Take on Legal Research · Access to justice · 2025

vlens.an: The supplied material builds on the proposition that an expanding legal-AI market requires disciplined selection and implementation rather than attention to announcements alone. Across these curated sources, the common reasoning is that buyers should examine day-to-day use, organisational readiness, workflow fit, security and privacy, and demonstrated business value before purchasing or renewing tools. The material makes the cluster’s prescription concrete through readiness assessments, adoption sprints, feature-level comparisons and go/no-go renewal reviews. There is material variation in depth: one source merely calls for scrutiny of actual attorney use; another develops a measured procurement and renewal process; and a third focuses on comparing narrowly defined use cases and product controls. The Garfield AI introduction illustrates market expansion but does not establish performance or operating-model success. Attribution is also important: much of the substantive commentary comes from podcast hosts and Legal Technology Hub representatives rather than the named AI-native providers themselves, and the evidence is advisory or promotional experience rather than quantified outcomes. Accordingly, this supports a concrete extension of the proposition but should not be treated as representative of AI-native legal providers generally.

qs.q: And we’re finding that those AI enablement projects often lead into further work around AI procurement, which I think is a really encouraging sign that the industry is moving beyond the FOMO and the push to buy something now and  figure out how to use it later.
qs.a: Greg Mazares Sr. on AI, E-Discovery, and the Future of Human-Led Legal Services · AI-native providers · 2026

qs.q: So buyers can see the grid and assess relatively quickly which of the products is more likely to suit their individual needs.

vlens.an: The curated Academia & research sources accept the principal proposition that legal AI is an expanding, increasingly complex market requiring disciplined, workflow-specific selection rather than reliance on product announcements alone. Wilkins makes the procurement prescription concrete through evaluation frameworks, use cases, pilot guides and requirements templates, while Shaver’s market-map data distinguishes product placements from vendors and identifies a reported shift in startup activity toward operational tools. The sources also consistently limit their conclusions: mapped growth is not treated as proof of adoption, revenue, productivity or client outcomes, and explanations such as crowding among broad assistants remain tentative. Material internal variation concerns scope rather than direction. Two sources primarily support market tracking and procurement discipline; the third extends the proposition into legal-service delivery by identifying AI-centred firms, including a partner-only model, as a prospective business-model development. That extension warrants Builds on overall, although its disruptive effects and comparative performance remain subjects for investigation rather than demonstrated findings. These sources are a curated set and should not be treated as representative of academia or research generally.

qs.q: For each premium category, we have a landscape overview, an evaluation framework, a use case, a pilot guide, a requirements template, and then any other information we think is important.

vlens.an: This curated legal-tech-vendor voice accepts the proposition that rapid market expansion requires disciplined selection and implementation, and materially develops it with concrete practices: needs assessment, workflow-specific comparison, vendor shortlisting, source-linked verification, scrutiny of usage costs and model choice, adoption support, governance enforcement, and controls for agentic systems. Common reasons include the proliferation and faster evolution of products, unresolved competition between frontier-model platforms and specialist tools, uneven organisational readiness, and the gap between deployment and effective workflow use. Material variation concerns emphasis rather than opposition: some sources focus narrowly on market mapping or promotional demonstrations; others add substantive procurement, cost, control and adoption criteria. A few redirect attention toward AI-led legal training or customer co-development, while introductory or unrelated excerpts remain unclear. Claims about productivity, product quality, funding and future growth are generally anecdotal, promotional or predictive rather than measured outcomes; no supplied source clearly opposes the proposition. These sources are a curated selection and should not be treated as representative of all legal-tech vendors.

qs.q: For example, if an agent is operating in a legal workflow, you may want to know whether visibility has been built in so that you can see the plan the agent creates for achieving its overall goal before it gets going on that plan and whether the lawyer or user is able to course correct the plan before it is executed.
qs.a: Laura Clayton McDonnell on Legal Technology, AI, and Corporate Transformation at Thomson Reuters · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

vlens.an: This curated set supports the proposition that an expanding and increasingly specialised legal-AI market requires disciplined selection and implementation rather than mere product acquisition. The sources give three complementary reasons: reported growth in the number and complexity of available products makes internal market tracking harder; the emergence of litigation-specific tools increases the need for workflow-specific evaluation; and licensing a tool does not itself produce adoption, because workload, culture and organisational readiness can impede use. There is material variation in emphasis—from portfolio management, to category-level product evaluation, to diagnosing implementation barriers—but no substantive disagreement with the proposition. The support is nevertheless limited: the relevant passages are chiefly promotional commentary from Legal Tech Hub’s Nikki Shaver, not substantive views from the law-firm figures named in the source titles; market-growth figures come from internal tracking, and the excerpts provide neither independent corroboration nor measured adoption, productivity or client outcomes. Accordingly, these records support the proposition but should not be treated as representative of traditional law firms generally.

qs.q: So…  Since 2023, especially, the legal tech market has ballooned in size and complexity.

vlens.an: The curated market-analyst, consultancy and press sources broadly support the proposition that legal AI is an expanding and increasingly complex market in which product activity must be distinguished from meaningful adoption, value and outcomes. Their recurring reasons are that mapped listings are growing but remain coverage-dependent; rapid feature development and specialised workflow entrants make comparison harder; reported usage metrics are definition-sensitive; and implementation requires internal skills, organisational structures and continuing market intelligence. Several sources add practical depth by identifying consumption-based pricing, token-use behaviour, confidentiality settings and workflow-specific buyer resources as matters for procurement and deployment scrutiny. Internal variation is material but does not change the overall direction: some contributions are qualitative market observations or promotional claims from Legal Technology Hub; some are forecasts about funding, competitive change or pricing rather than demonstrated outcomes; and two excerpts merely preview discussions or address the peripheral prospect of premium-priced judgment, leaving their position unclear. The sources do not collectively establish market-wide adoption, productivity, revenue, savings or comparative product performance, and this curated set should not be treated as representative of all analysts, consultancies or press.

elens.an: The 2025 sources collectively accept the cluster’s principal proposition and materially develop its practical implications. They describe a rapidly expanding and unstable product landscape, but repeatedly distinguish directory growth, funding, product announcements and self-reported use from demonstrated adoption, performance, revenue or value. Their common response is disciplined, workflow-specific selection and implementation: define the business problem, assess organisational needs, compare relevant features, security, privacy and hosting, conduct demonstrations and shortlisting, train users, and enforce governance policies. Several sources add concrete extensions, including procurement methods for transaction management and specialised fund workflows, segment-specific support for heterogeneous mid-sized firms, verification through source-linked market research, confidentiality controls, and capability-based scrutiny of agentic products—especially whether users can inspect and redirect an agent’s plan before execution. Material variation lies mainly in emphasis and evidentiary strength. Some sources focus narrowly on expanding market maps or funding and therefore only support the proposition’s market-complexity premise; others directly develop procurement, adoption or governance practices. Several promotional openings make optimistic productivity or market forecasts without measured outcomes, while sources on rollout versus adoption and ambiguous survey definitions reinforce caution about adoption claims. A number of excerpts are merely introductions, career observations or unrelated announcements and leave their position unclear. No supplied source clearly opposes the proposition, but this curated set should not be treated as representative or its source counts as evidence of prevalence.

qs.q: For example, if an agent is operating in a legal workflow, you may want to know whether visibility has been built in so that you can see the plan the agent creates for achieving its overall goal before it gets going on that plan and whether the lawyer or user is able to course correct the plan before it is executed.
qs.a: Laura Clayton McDonnell on Legal Technology, AI, and Corporate Transformation at Thomson Reuters · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

elens.an:
The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that a larger, faster-changing legal-AI market requires disciplined selection and implementation, and they materially develop it in several concrete directions. Common reasons include the proliferation of mapped products and features; big-tech and frontier-model providers entering legal workflows; unresolved choices between general-purpose platforms and specialist tools; and the practical separation of purchase, deployment, day-to-day use and realised value. The sources add procurement criteria covering workflow fit, readiness, renewal value, model and context-window selection, consumption-based pricing, token overages, infrastructure control and user agency. They also extend the market-maturity argument to emerging AI-centred law-firm models, while treating their effects as prospective rather than demonstrated.

Material internal variation concerns emphasis and evidentiary strength rather than broad rejection. Several sources merely support market awareness through maps, portfolio tools, geographic filtering or curated demonstrations; others provide more substantial implementation frameworks through readiness assessments, workflow sprints and value-based renewal reviews. Some redirect attention toward legal training or vendor-side customer co-development, while excerpts on trusted judgment, smaller firms and conference activity are too limited to establish a position. No supplied source clearly opposes the proposition. Much of the evidence comes from Legal Technology Hub personnel in promotional podcast openings and reflects directory tracking, advisory experience, announcements or forecasts rather than independent performance studies. Accordingly, reported product placements should not be read as equivalent to launches, adoption or revenue, and claims about consolidation, pricing diffusion and business-model transformation remain predictions or exploratory observations.
